clue.text: Sign of importance to Mallarmeé and Verlaine

definitions.text: Sign of importance to Mallarmeé and Verlaine

parts.words: Sign of importance to Mallarmeé and Verlaine
parts.note: a sign or emblem, here the key notion of the French poetic movement those two poets led

explanation.surface: A token that mattered greatly to two French poets.
explanation.walkthrough: Mallarmé and Verlaine were leading French Symbolist poets of the late nineteenth century.
explanation.definitionFit: An emblem standing for something else is the central idea of the movement named after it, to which both poets belonged.

clue.text: Swift computer directory? ()

explanation.surface: A quick list kept on a computer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swift' looks like an adjective meaning fast; it is Jonathan Swift, author of Gulliver's Travels.
explanation.definitionFit: Swift's Gulliver meets brutish human beasts of that name; a well-known web portal began as a directory of internet sites.

clue.text: Bolt hound, perhaps, for such field sport from Neil Gunn

definitions.text: such field sport from Neil Gunn

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters given might be some other arrangement of themselves

explanation.surface: A hound that bolts might suit the hunting in a Scottish novelist's book.
explanation.walkthrough: BOLTHOUND rearranged gives the title of a 1952 novel by the Scottish writer Neil Gunn.
explanation.definitionFit: Neil Gunn's novel is named for a pursuit to the death, a hunting sport of the field.

clue.text: "Tell me what thy name is on the Night's Plutonian shore!" (Edgar Allan Poe) Sheridan character describing our Prime Minis ter at his most positive?

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held is the Poe quotation 'Tell me what thy ... name is on the Night's Plutonian shore!' with the missing word not shown and 5-down's clue appended; the clue is garbled and shown on two lights.
annotationWithheld.clue: "Tell me what thy name is on the Night's Plutonian shore!" (Edgar Allan Poe) Sheridan character describing our Prime Minis ter at his most positive?

clue.text: "! tis the hour of prayer!" (Byron)

parts.note: a line of Byron's Don Juan with its opening Latin words of a Catholic prayer to the Virgin missing, to be supplied

explanation.surface: A line from Byron announcing the time for prayer.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is a fill-in quotation: the words missing before the exclamation mark open Byron's line in Don Juan, canto III.
explanation.definitionFit: Byron's line begins with the Latin salutation to the Virgin that names the evening prayer bell.

clue.text: Sheridan character describing our Prime Minister at his most positive?

parts.note: Tony Blair, Prime Minister when the puzzle appeared, has the full first name Anthony
absolute means utterly certain, as positive as can be

explanation.surface: A stage character who sums up the Prime Minister when he is most sure of himself.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Anthony Absolute is the domineering father in Sheridan's comedy The Rivals; Tony Blair was Britain's Prime Minister at the time.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Anthony Absolute is a role in Sheridan's play The Rivals.

clue.text: Church historian whose letters are distributed haphazardly (ie, bus use?)

indicators.note: scattered at random, so the letters of the bracketed words are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A churchman whose name is a muddle of a few short words.
explanation.walkthrough: IEBUSUSE rearranged gives the name of the fourth-century bishop of Caesarea who wrote the first history of the Church.
explanation.definitionFit: Eusebius of Caesarea wrote the Ecclesiastical History, the earliest surviving chronicle of early Christianity.

clue.text: Llewelyn Powys wanted fruit of this sort to be mature

definitions.text: Llewelyn Powys wanted fruit of this sort to be mature

parts.words: Llewelyn Powys wanted fruit of this sort to be mature
parts.note: points to a Llewelyn Powys novel whose title says a kind of orchard fruit should be ripe

explanation.surface: A writer hoping his orchard crop would ripen.
explanation.walkthrough: Llewelyn Powys published the novel Apples Be Ripe in 1930.
explanation.definitionFit: The Powys title names the common orchard fruit as the one that should be ripe.

clue.text: Laid it on a bit thick, artistically

definitions.text: Laid it on a bit thick, artistically

parts.words: Laid it on a bit thick, artistically
parts.note: reads as exaggerating, but means a painter applied paint in a heavy textured layer

explanation.surface: Someone overdid things, with an artistic flourish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Laid it on a bit thick' suggests exaggeration; literally it is a painter's thick application of oil paint.
explanation.definitionFit: Impasto is the technique of applying paint thickly so brush or knife marks stand out.

clue.text: The strange citrous Greek poet produced

indicators.note: strange suggests something odd or out of order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Something odd and lemony has been produced by a classical poet.
explanation.walkthrough: THECITROUS rearranged gives the Sicilian Greek poet credited with inventing pastoral verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Theocritus, writing in the third century BC, is the father of Greek pastoral poetry.

clue.text: Wells's coachbuilder who fathered Romola

parts.note: points to the retired coachbuilder in H. G. Wells's novel Marriage, father of several daughters

explanation.surface: A craftsman in a Wells novel who was father to a girl named after an Eliot heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Romola' suggests George Eliot's novel; here it is one of the daughters of Mr Pope in H. G. Wells's Marriage (1912).
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Pope, the retired coachbuilder in Wells's Marriage, is the father of the heroine and her sisters.

clue.text: "When it was written, God and Robert Browning knew what it meant; now only God knows"

definitions.text: "When it was written, God and Robert Browning knew what it meant; now only God knows"

parts.words: "When it was written, God and Robert Browning knew what it meant; now only God knows"
parts.note: a famous quip about an obscure long poem by Browning that even its author could no longer explain

explanation.surface: A jibe about a poem so baffling only the Almighty understands it.
explanation.walkthrough: The remark, often attributed to Browning himself, refers to his notoriously difficult 1840 poem about an Italian troubadour.
explanation.definitionFit: Browning's long poem Sordello was mocked as incomprehensible, the target of this famous quip.

clue.text: A kind of stroke by Molly Parkin

definitions.text: A kind of stroke by Molly Parkin

parts.words: A kind of stroke by Molly Parkin
parts.note: points to a Molly Parkin novel named after a swimming style

explanation.surface: A swimming technique attributed to a novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: Molly Parkin, a Welsh novelist and artist, published the comic novel Breast Stroke in 1975.
explanation.definitionFit: Parkin's title names the swimming stroke done face down with frog-like kicks.

clue.text: He paid dearly for his brother's lentil soup

definitions.text: He paid dearly for his brother's lentil soup

parts.words: He paid dearly for his brother's lentil soup
parts.note: refers to the Genesis story of a hungry hunter trading his birthright for a bowl of pottage

explanation.surface: A man who overpaid for a family meal.
explanation.walkthrough: In Genesis 25, Jacob's elder twin sells his birthright for a dish of red lentil stew.
explanation.definitionFit: Esau, Jacob's twin, gave up his birthright for a bowl of lentils.

clue.text: Desmond Bagley's attempt to mislead cat?

parts.note: to snow someone is to deceive or overwhelm them with smooth talk
a tiger is a big cat

explanation.surface: A thriller writer's ploy to fool a feline.
explanation.walkthrough: Desmond Bagley was a British thriller writer; The Snow Tiger (1975) is one of his novels.
explanation.definitionFit: The Snow Tiger is a novel by the thriller writer Desmond Bagley.

clue.text: The immature cat of Forrest Reid?

parts.note: young means not yet grown up
a tom is a male cat

explanation.surface: An Irish novelist's kitten.
explanation.walkthrough: Forrest Reid, the Belfast novelist, wrote Young Tom (1944), about a boy growing up in Ulster.
explanation.definitionFit: Young Tom is a novel by Forrest Reid about a boy's childhood.

clue.text: Not ignore (wrongly) Eliot's view of old age

indicators.note: wrongly means done in error, so the letters are set out in a mistaken order

explanation.surface: A plea not to overlook what a poet thought about growing old.
explanation.walkthrough: NOTIGNORE rearranged gives the title of T. S. Eliot's 1920 poem, a Greek-derived word for a little old man.
explanation.definitionFit: Eliot's poem Gerontion is the monologue of an old man reflecting on age and history.

clue.text: Sylvia Ashton-Warner's bookish old maid

parts.note: points to the New Zealand writer's first novel, titled after an unmarried woman

explanation.surface: An unmarried, studious woman in a New Zealand author's work.
explanation.walkthrough: Sylvia Ashton-Warner's 1958 novel, about a teacher in a Maori school, carries this title; 'bookish' signals that it is a book.
explanation.definitionFit: An unmarried older woman is traditionally so called, and it is the title of Ashton-Warner's novel.

clue.text: Novel account of Dylan Thomas's local?

definitions.text: Novel account of Dylan Thomas's local?

parts.words: Novel account of Dylan Thomas's local?
parts.note: a pub frequented by a Welsh poet could be named this, which is also the title of an Eric Linklater novel

explanation.surface: A fresh story about the Welsh poet's favourite bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like 'new'; it means a book: Poet's Pub (1929) by Eric Linklater. A 'local' is a British regular pub.
explanation.definitionFit: Dylan Thomas, a poet famous for drinking, had a regular pub; Linklater's novel bears that description as its title.

clue.text: Dire version of Chiantishire poet

indicators.note: a version of a word can be another arrangement of its letters

explanation.surface: A grim retelling by a poet from Tuscany.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chiantishire' is a joking British name for Tuscany; Francesco Redi wrote the Tuscan dithyramb Bacco in Toscana.
explanation.definitionFit: Francesco Redi was a seventeenth-century Tuscan poet and scientist, Tuscany being nicknamed after its Chianti wine.

clue.text: Witches come up in sly bishop's remarks

indicators.note: in a down entry, coming up means the letters read from bottom to top
in shows the letters sit inside the run of words that follow

explanation.surface: Witches surface in a crafty cleric's comments.
explanation.walkthrough: SLYBIS lies in 'sly bishop's'; 'come up' turns it round, since this is a down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Sibyls were prophetesses of the ancient world, women credited with supernatural foresight like witches.

clue.text: Origin of word in Society (monthly publication)

indicators.note: in signals the letters lie within the words that follow

explanation.surface: A word's source appears in a society's monthly magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: ETYMON straddles 'Society' and 'monthly'.
explanation.definitionFit: An etymon is the earlier form from which a word is derived, its root.

clue.text: Time of bucolic break for Turgenev?

definitions.text: Time of bucolic break for Turgenev?

parts.words: Time of bucolic break for Turgenev?
parts.note: points to Turgenev's play about a period spent out of town

explanation.surface: How long the Russian writer took for a rural holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: Turgenev's comedy is A Month in the Country (1850); 'bucolic break' is the stay in the country.
explanation.definitionFit: A Month in the Country names a period of about thirty days, the length of the play's rural interlude.

clue.text: For Coward, the Brighton Pavilion looked like such a tart

definitions.text: For Coward, the Brighton Pavilion looked like such a tart

parts.words: For Coward, the Brighton Pavilion looked like such a tart
parts.note: alludes to Noel Coward's quip comparing the Prince Regent's eastern-style palace to an exotic woman of easy virtue

explanation.surface: A playwright's barbed comment on a seaside palace's showy look.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Pavilion at Brighton, a seaside town, was built for the Prince Regent in an Indian and Chinese style; 'tart' reads as pastry but means a loose woman.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pavilion's domes and minarets are in an Eastern, Asian style, hence the exotic comparison.

clue.text: Jewish men of letters start with it

definitions.text: Jewish men of letters start with it

parts.words: Jewish men of letters start with it
parts.note: reads as Jewish writers, but means the alphabet a Hebrew scribe uses begins with this character

explanation.surface: Jewish writers begin with this.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Men of letters' suggests authors; the letters are those of the Hebrew alphabet, whose first is this.
explanation.definitionFit: Aleph is the opening letter of the Hebrew alphabet.

clue.text: A turn to the North for Greek games

parts.note: a go is a turn in a game
N is the abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: A trip northwards to see some Hellenic sport.
explanation.walkthrough: In ancient Greece an agon was a contest or public games.
explanation.definitionFit: An agon was a contest in ancient Greece, whether athletic, musical or dramatic.

clue.text: Richard Cobden thought that The Times contained more useful information than all this historian's works

definitions.text: Richard Cobden thought that The Times contained more useful information than all this historian's works

parts.words: Richard Cobden thought that The Times contained more useful information than all this historian's works
parts.note: refers to the Victorian free-trader's remark dismissing a classical Greek historian of the Peloponnesian War

explanation.surface: A politician's claim that a newspaper beat an ancient chronicler for usefulness.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Cobden, the nineteenth-century Radical MP, said one copy of The Times held more useful information than the whole of Thucydides.
explanation.definitionFit: Thucydides wrote the history of the Peloponnesian War, the work Cobden belittled.

clue.text: Reran the revisions for devout poet

indicators.note: revisions are reworkings, so these letters are reworked into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone reran the edits for a religious poet.
explanation.walkthrough: RERANTHE rearranged gives Thomas Traherne, the seventeenth-century mystical poet and clergyman.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Traherne was a seventeenth-century clergyman whose poems celebrate divine joy and childhood innocence.

clue.text: Familiar name of errant Spanish squire

definitions.text: Familiar name of errant Spanish squire

parts.words: Familiar name of errant Spanish squire
parts.note: points to the first name of Don Quixote's squire, companion of the knight errant

explanation.surface: What a wandering Spanish attendant is usually called.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Errant' refers to Don Quixote the knight errant; his squire is Sancho Panza, usually called by his first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Sancho Panza, squire to Don Quixote in Cervantes's novel, is known by his first name.
